strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem in joint video super-resolution and deblurring: dynamically varying exposure, which is common in auto-exposure and low-light capture. The proposed Exposure Time-aware Modulation and exposure-aware FGDF are plausible components for conditioning restoration on exposure-related context.

The core architectural contribution, Hierarchical Refinement with Bidirectional Propagation (HRBP), is well motivated and empirically supported. The ablations show that the hierarchical design improves both accuracy and temporal consistency over sliding-window and recurrent alternatives while enabling sequence-level parallelization and faster inference.

The method achieves strong quantitative results on the proposed REDS4-ME benchmarks and on GoPro, with notable gains over the retrained FMA-Net* baseline. The efficiency improvements are also meaningful, e.g., 0.074s per LR frame versus 0.318s for FMA-Net*, while using only a modest increase in parameters.

The paper introduces REDS-ME and REDS-RE benchmarks for multi-exposure and random-exposure VSRDB, which help standardize evaluation under changing exposure. The experimental section includes extensive ablations on temporal modeling, exposure conditioning, HRBP depth, multi-flow-mask pairs, loss terms, and filtering mechanisms.

The supplementary material provides useful details on the physical degradation model, training strategy, dataset generation, and limitations. The discussion of real-world qualitative results, while not quantitatively grounded, supports the claim that the method generalizes better than fixed-exposure baselines.

The work is clearly written and well organized, with sufficient implementation details for reproducibility in the supplementary. The paper appropriately acknowledges key limitations, including synthetic dataset limitations and flow-based motion modeling.
weaknesses: The contribution is incremental relative to FMA-Net (CVPR 2024). Several core components, including FGDF, iterative feature refinement, and multi-attention, are inherited or adapted from the predecessor. The main new components, ETM and exposure-aware FGDF, are extensions of existing conditioning and dynamic filtering ideas rather than fundamentally new formulations.

Exposure modeling is not directly grounded in physical exposure time. The ETE is trained with pseudo exposure labels derived from synthetic frame averaging and may entangle exposure with motion, blur severity, and scene content. The paper does not explicitly estimate exposure time at test time, and the reported gains from ETE on in-distribution REDS-ME are small (about 0.1 dB), although the out-of-distribution gains are larger.

The proposed REDS-ME and REDS-RE benchmarks are synthetic derivatives of REDS. They simulate exposure changes by averaging interpolated high-frame-rate frames and do not model nonlinear camera response, sensor noise, spatially varying illumination, or true continuous auto-exposure. Real-world evaluation lacks ground truth and relies on no-reference metrics and qualitative examples.

Some experimental details for fair comparison are insufficiently described in the main paper, e.g., how event data are simulated for Ev-DeblurVSR and how all baselines are adapted/retrained. This affects confidence in the exact fairness of the comparisons, especially for methods that were not originally designed for VSRDB under dynamic exposure.

The HRBP architecture is compared mainly against sliding-window and recurrent variants, with limited discussion of other hierarchical or multi-scale propagation methods in video restoration. The ablation contributions of individual components are relatively small in some cases, and the full model is only marginally better than a more expensive FGDF-based low-frequency prediction variant in Table 5, weakening the efficiency-vs-accuracy argument slightly.

The real-world generalization evidence is limited: only a few qualitative examples are shown, without quantitative evaluation on real captured multi-exposure videos with ground truth. The title and abstract emphasize real-world restoration, but the primary quantitative evidence remains synthetic. The claims could be more carefully scoped accordingly.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored problem: joint video super-resolution and deblurring under unknown, dynamically varying exposure, with new benchmarks REDS-ME and REDS-RE derived from REDS.

Proposes a coherent framework with Exposure Time-aware Modulation (ETM) and Hierarchical Refinement with Bidirectional Propagation (HRBP), supported by thorough ablations on ETM, HRBP depth, multi-flow masks, attention design, loss coefficients, and FGDF vs conventional dynamic filtering.

Reports strong quantitative results: state-of-the-art PSNR/SSIM/tOF on REDS-ME, REDS-RE, and zero-shot GoPro, with notable gains on out-of-distribution settings (e.g., +1.66 dB PSNR on GoPro over FMA-Net*).
Provides extensive implementation details and supplementary analyses, including t-SNE of exposure features, kernel visualizations, flow visualizations, and qualitative real-world examples.
Discusses limitations candidly, including synthetic benchmark construction and 2D flow-based motion modeling.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely incremental over FMA-Net: ETM is a feature-modulation layer conditioned on exposure embeddings, and HRBP is a hierarchical propagation variant; architectural novelty is limited for a top-tier conference.

The central claim of handling unknown, dynamically varying exposure in real-world videos is not quantitatively validated: real-world results are qualitative only, and the proposed benchmarks are synthetic with discrete exposure levels, whereas real auto-exposure is continuous.

The Exposure Time-aware Feature Extractor (ETE) is trained on synthetic discrete exposure labels and may not disentangle exposure from motion/content cues; no analysis is provided to show that the learned embeddings capture exposure rather than blur severity or scene motion.

Benchmark construction via high-frame-rate frame averaging may not faithfully model real camera motion blur (e.g., nonlinear sensor response, spatially varying illumination, sensor noise), which limits the validity of the benchmark as a proxy for real-world exposure variation.

The comparison to Ev-DeblurVSR in Table 1 is questionable because the method requires event data unavailable in standard RGB videos; the paper does not clearly explain how it was retrained/adapted, making the comparison potentially misleading.
Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of a code/dataset release statement, despite the paper introducing new benchmarks.

Some equations and notation are dense and potentially confusing, particularly the high-dimensional degradation kernel formulation and how the predicted kernel is actually applied in the filtering operation.

Performance gains over FMA-Net on REDS-ME are modest (~0.6 dB PSNR), and the efficiency advantage is mainly relative to the sliding-window FMA-Net; FMA-Net++ remains slower than some baselines such as BasicVSR++.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored and practically important problem: joint VSRDB under unknown, frame-wise varying exposure, motivated by real auto-exposure/low-light capture conditions. The paper correctly observes that most prior VSRDB work assumes a fixed exposure time, which is a real gap.

The paper provides a physically motivated formulation of the degradation process (Eq. 7-10 in supplement), coupling exposure time and motion into a spatio-temporally varying blur kernel. Grounding the network's kernel prediction in this physical model (via the ETM-conditioned FGDF) is a principled design choice rather than an ad-hoc module.

The decoupled two-network design (Net^D for exposure/motion-aware degradation priors, Net^R for guided restoration) is conceptually clean, allows independent supervision of each stage, and yields good efficiency (12.8M params, ~0.074 s runtime) while being competitive or better than much larger baselines (e.g., BSSTNet* with 52M params).

The HRBP block is a sensible engineering contribution: sequence-level parallelism with hierarchical receptive-field expansion addresses concrete limitations of sliding-window (limited receptive field) and recurrent (sequential, gradient vanishing) approaches. The comparison in Fig. 2(a) and the ablation in Table 3 concretely demonstrate the benefit.

Comprehensive experiments: comparisons on REDS4-ME, REDS-RE, GoPro, plus real-world smartphone videos; ablations on ETM, HRBP depth, multi-flow-mask count, DA attention, upsampling choice, and loss coefficients. The ETM sensitivity analysis (Table 6) and t-SNE of exposure features (Fig. 8) provide useful diagnostic evidence.

The two new benchmarks (REDS-ME and REDS-RE) are well-motivated and clearly documented (Sec. 8.2 of supplement), and the structured random-walk exposure trajectory in REDS-RE is a more realistic simulation of auto-exposure behavior than frame-wise randomization. These could be a useful community resource.

Strong generalization story: training solely on synthetic data and evaluating on unseen GoPro and real smartphone videos with continuous auto-exposure transitions (Fig. 15), which is a meaningful practical validation.

The supplement is thorough, with full derivations, training strategy details, and additional qualitative/quantitative analyses. Limitations are honestly discussed (synthetic averaging model, 2D flow limitations).
weaknesses: The physical-grounding claim is somewhat overstated. The ETE must infer per-frame exposure time from the blurry LR input, but the degradation process itself destroys exposure information; the paper's own t-SNE (Fig. 8) shows that exposure levels 5:4 and 5:5 — the two levels used at evaluation — are the least separable, which is precisely where reliable conditioning matters most. The reported gains on REDS4-ME are correspondingly modest (e.g., 29.24 vs. 28.51 PSNR for FMA-Net* on 5:5, and 29.66 vs. 29.04 on 5:4), which weakens the claim that the model is truly exposure-aware rather than simply a stronger backbone.

The novelty of the individual components is moderate. The ETM is an SFT-style affine modulation (Wang et al. [47]) conditioned on a learned embedding; the exposure-aware FGDF is a natural extension of FMA-Net's FGDF; the HRBP is a hierarchical multi-scale extension of existing bidirectional propagation ideas (BasicVSR++, RVRT, etc.). The paper would benefit from a clearer statement of what is genuinely new versus what is a well-chosen combination of existing primitives.

The exposure-aware conditioning signal used during training is derived from synthetic exposure labels; on real videos with continuous auto-exposure, the discrete 5:1..5:5 anchors may not span the true distribution. While the supplement argues that the feature space interpolates smoothly, this is asserted rather than rigorously verified, and the real-world evaluation is limited to no-reference metrics (NIQE/MUSIQ) on a small set of clips.

Fairness of comparisons is not fully established. Baselines are marked with '*' to indicate retraining on REDS-ME, but it is unclear whether all baselines received comparable tuning effort, batch sizes, and iteration counts. Methods like IART* and BSSTNet* are VSR/deblurring methods not designed for VSRDB and are given blurry inputs, which arguably stacks the deck. The event-based Ev-DeblurVSR requires inputs FMA-Net++ cannot use, so its comparison is only partially informative.

The synthetic degradation used to build REDS-ME (linear averaging of high-frame-rate frames) is acknowledged as a simplification; it does not model spatially varying lighting, sensor noise, or nonlinear sensor response, all of which are tightly coupled with exposure in real capture. This limits the strength of the claim that REDS-ME is a faithful benchmark for 'real-world' dynamic exposure.

No quantitative evaluation on real-world data with ground truth (only qualitative + no-reference metrics). For a paper whose central claim is real-world robustness under dynamic exposure, this is a notable gap.

The 2D optical flow backbone (RAFT-based) is acknowledged to fail under large out-of-plane rotations and non-rigid motion; the multi-flow-mask mechanism mitigates but does not solve this. The paper does not quantify how often this failure mode affects the reported results.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: joint VSRDB under frame-wise exposure-duration variation, a setting largely overlooked by prior fixed-exposure methods (e.g., FMA-Net, BasicVSR++, VRT).

The proposed HRBA backbone offers a clean architectural solution that combines sequence-level parallelism with hierarchically expanding temporal receptive fields, avoiding both the limited receptive field of sliding-window designs and the sequential bottleneck of recurrent ones. The efficiency gains are concrete (12.8M params, 0.074s runtime, 6.2 GB memory vs. VRT's 35.6M / 0.684s / 20.5 GB).

The Exposure Time-aware Modulation (ETM) layer and ETE feature extractor provide a physically grounded mechanism (Eq. 1-3) to condition degradation kernels on exposure, supported by kernel-shape visualizations (Fig. 7b) and t-SNE clustering (Fig. 7a).

Comprehensive experimental validation: two new benchmarks (REDS-ME, REDS-RE) plus GoPro and real-world smartphone videos, with numerous ablations covering temporal strategy (Table 3), ETE design (Tables 4-7), HRBA depth and DA attention (Table 8), number of multi-flow-mask pairs, loss coefficients, and exposure-aware FGDF.

Ablation studies are thoughtful and honest: e.g., the capacity-matched w/o-ETE baseline (13.1M) isolates the effect of exposure modeling from backbone capacity, and the corruption experiments on guidance (Tables 6, 7) probe whether ETE guidance is actually used.
Clear writing, good figures, and a clear decoupling of degradation learning from restoration, which is well-articulated in the method section.
weaknesses: The contribution is incremental relative to FMA-Net (CVPR 2024): the two main deltas are (i) replacing the sliding-window backbone with HRBA and (ii) adding an exposure-conditioned FiLM-style modulation. Neither is a fundamentally new idea; HRBA resembles prior hierarchical refinement designs, and ETM is a standard feature-modulation layer.

The exposure modeling is built on a synthetic discretization into five duty-cycle levels (5:1 to 5:5). Real-world exposure is continuous, and the ETE is trained with discrete pseudo-labels; generalization to continuous exposure is only argued (Sec. S5.2) and shown qualitatively, not quantitatively validated. This is a substantive gap given the paper's core premise.

Improvement margins over the strongest baselines are modest in places (e.g., +0.62/+0.73 dB over FMA-Net* on REDS-ME-5:4/5:5; HRBA at 29.24 vs. recurrent variant at 29.11 in Table 3). The recurrent variant being nearly on par with HRBA weakens the claimed necessity of the hierarchical design, and the paper does not analyze this.

The new benchmarks (REDS-ME, REDS-RE) are synthesized by frame-averaging interpolated REDS frames, inheriting the standard blur-then-downsample assumption. They are useful but do not constitute an independent, real-capture benchmark; the 'state-of-the-art' claims are therefore largely on self-constructed synthetic data.

No controlled evaluation of ETE robustness to exposure distributions outside the 5 anchors, and no discussion of what happens under over/under-exposure, ISO changes, or clipping — the limitations section acknowledges these but the impact on the core claims is not measured.

Some design choices (e.g., freezing ETE, contrastive pre-training, multi-flow-mask initialization with f=0, o=1) appear somewhat ad hoc and are justified primarily by end-task performance rather than principled reasoning.
Societal-impact discussion is absent (minor for this task, but noted for completeness).

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and under-explored problem: joint video super-resolution and deblurring under frame-wise exposure-duration variation, which is a genuine issue in real footage.

Introduces two new benchmarks (REDS-ME and REDS-RE) that provide a controlled testbed for exposure-varying VSRDB, which could be useful to the community even if the synthetic degradations are simplified.

The HRBA backbone is a reasonable architectural choice that enables sequence-level parallel temporal aggregation while expanding the temporal receptive field, and the ablation in Table 3 shows it outperforms both sliding-window and recurrent variants.

Extensive experimental evaluation: many baselines, two exposure benchmarks, GoPro generalization, ablation studies on temporal modeling, ETE design, kernel guidance, capacity matching, and multi-flow-mask pairs.
ETE shows meaningful gains on out-of-distribution data (GoPro: +0.64 dB over the capacity-matched baseline), suggesting exposure conditioning does help when exposure truly varies.
Some honest reporting (e.g., acknowledging that the capacity-matched w/o-ETE model absorbs most of the in-distribution PSNR gain, and the limitations section on ISO/noise/white balance).
weaknesses: Incremental contribution: FMA-Net++ is essentially the authors' prior CVPR 2024 FMA-Net augmented with (i) a hierarchical backbone and (ii) exposure conditioning. The '+' naming and framing read as a journal-style extension rather than a new ECCV-worthy contribution.

The paper's headline novelty (exposure-aware ETM/ETE) provides only marginal in-distribution gain: Table 4 shows 29.20 (capacity-matched w/o ETE) vs. 29.24 (w/ ETE) on REDS4-ME-5:5, i.e., ~0.04 dB, with the capacity-matched baseline even winning on 5:4. The authors themselves note that most of the in-distribution gain comes from backbone capacity rather than exposure modeling.

The new benchmarks are self-created and self-serving: the synthesized blur is obtained by frame averaging of interpolated high-frame-rate frames, ignoring ISO/gain, clipping, sensor noise, white-balance shifts, and spatially varying illumination. The model is therefore evaluated primarily on a degradation that the authors designed and that matches their assumptions.

Real-world evaluation is weak: only a handful of smartphone clips are shown, with no-reference metrics (NIQE/MUSIQ) whose reliability as a proxy for restoration quality is limited and which are reported on selected examples rather than a comprehensive test set.

The HRBA design (hierarchical bidirectional aggregation over expanding temporal neighborhoods) is conceptually similar to well-established ideas in video restoration (e.g., pyramid/hierarchical temporal aggregation, bidirectional multi-scale propagation), so the architectural novelty is limited.

The 'unknown exposure time' problem is not new: prior work in video deblurring and frame interpolation has addressed unknown/varying exposure (e.g., EvDeblurVSR, event-based deblurring, exposure-aware frame interpolation), and the paper's physical formulation (Eq. 1) is the standard blur model.

Fair comparison is difficult to assess: many baselines (and the authors' own FMA-Net*) are retrained on the authors' synthetic REDS-ME training set, which could favor the proposed model; the gap between FMA-Net* and FMA-Net++ is largely attributable to HRBA, not to the claimed exposure-aware component.

Limited theoretical contribution: the mapping from exposure/motion to the degradation kernel is presented as an intractable inverse problem, and the proposed solution is a learned approximation with no analysis of identifiability or guarantees.

Reproducibility details (data synthesis, contrastive loss, hyperparameters) are largely relegated to the supplementary, and the exact composition of the exposure trajectories in REDS-RE is defined by a hand-crafted random walk, which may not reflect real camera auto-exposure behavior.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored and practically relevant problem: joint video super-resolution and deblurring under frame-wise varying exposure time, which is common in auto-exposure camera systems yet largely assumed fixed in prior VSRDB work.

The HRBA (Hierarchical Refinement with Bidirectional Aggregation) block is a well-motivated architectural design that jointly avoids the limited receptive field of sliding-window methods and the sequential bottleneck of recurrent methods, enabling sequence-level parallelism. The conceptual comparison in Fig. 2(a) clearly situates it among alternatives.

The Exposure Time-aware Modulation (ETM) layer together with the contrastive ETE is a clean mechanism for injecting per-frame exposure information into the degradation estimation pipeline. The ablation on ETE design (Table 5) and the frame-wise guidance corruption test (Table 6) provide strong evidence that the exposure signal is actively used rather than trivially absorbed by backbone capacity.

Comprehensive and honest evaluation: SOTA results on REDS4-ME, REDS-RE, and GoPro, with ablations covering temporal modeling variants, number of HRBA blocks, multi-flow-mask pairs, loss coefficients, and exposure-conditioning alternatives. The capacity-matched w/o-ETE baseline (13.1M) is a particularly fair and informative control.

The two new benchmarks (REDS-ME and REDS-RE) are a useful community contribution, with a clearly documented synthesis pipeline (blur-then-downsample, EMA-VFI interpolation, duty-cycle-defined exposure levels, structured random-walk exposure trajectories in Algorithm S1) that is reproducible and well-justified.
Strong efficiency story: 5.2x speedup over RVRT and substantially lower memory (6.2 GB vs 20.5 GB for VRT on 10-frame 180x320), supported by concrete runtime and parameter counts in Table 1.

Qualitative generalization to real-world smartphone videos with continuous exposure changes and no-reference metrics (NIQE/MUSIQ) demonstrates practical value beyond the synthetic training distribution, and the t-SNE/confusion-matrix analysis of ETE embeddings (Fig. 7a, Fig. S2) supports the claimed ordinal exposure representation.
Limitations are explicitly discussed (S6), and the physical degradation formulation in Sec. 3.1 provides a principled motivation for the learnable kernel approximation.
weaknesses: Incrementality over FMA-Net (CVPR 2024): the FGDF module and overall decoupled degradation-learning/restoration paradigm are inherited, and the primary new components are the HRBA backbone and ETM. The contribution is a meaningful but relatively bounded extension rather than a fundamentally new framework.

Quantitative gains over the retrained FMA-Net* are modest (e.g., 0.62 dB / 0.73 dB PSNR on REDS4-ME 5:4 and 5:5, and smaller margins on GoPro), which somewhat weakens the case that the new architecture is decisively better rather than a refinement.

The new benchmarks are synthetic (derived from REDS with an EMA-VFI-based synthesis), so the claim of 'controlled exposure-duration variation' is only as valid as the synthesis assumption; the paper acknowledges that other camera factors (ISO/gain, clipping, white balance, sensor noise) are excluded, which limits realism.

Real-world evaluation is restricted to qualitative visualizations and no-reference metrics; there is no quantitative ground-truth comparison on genuinely captured dynamic-exposure data, so the out-of-distribution robustness claim rests primarily on synthetic and perceptual evidence.

All baselines marked with * are retrained on the REDS-ME training set; while this is reasonable for fairness, the paper does not fully characterize how sensitive these retrained baselines are to the retraining protocol, and the comparison against the original FMA-Net (non-retrained) is not isolated from this effect.

The choice of exposure levels is discretized to five anchors (5:1 to 5:5), and the ETE is pretrained only on these discrete pseudo-labels. Although the ordinal structure is argued to allow interpolation, the handling of truly continuous exposure at test time is asserted rather than quantitatively measured.

Some design decisions (e.g., n=9 multi-flow-mask pairs, k_d=20 kernel size, M=4 HRBA blocks) are chosen from ablation trends, but the sensitivity to the ETE anchor set and to the exposure-level discretization granularity is not explored.
